sections.authorBiography: Nathaniel Hawthorne was born in Salem, Massachusetts, on 4 July 1804; his ancestor John Hathorne was a judge in the Salem witch trials of 1692, a family history Hawthorne felt as a burden. He later changed the spelling of his surname to Hawthorne; why is uncertain, though many link it to his discomfort with his ancestors. After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 he spent years writing in near-seclusion in Salem, publishing Twice-Told Tales in 1837. He lived briefly at the utopian Brook Farm community, worked at the Salem Custom House, and achieved fame with The Scarlet Letter (1850) and The House of the Seven Gables (1851). He served as U.S. consul in Liverpool and died on 19 May 1864 in Plymouth, New Hampshire.
sections.historicalContext: The novel is set in Puritan Boston in the 1640s, about twenty years after the founding of the Massachusetts Bay Colony (1630). The Puritan colony joined church and civil authority: magistrates punished moral offenses such as adultery publicly, and colonial laws allowed for punishments including whipping, the pillory and, in some periods, the wearing of letters. Real figures appear: Governor Richard Bellingham, the minister John Wilson, Mistress Ann Hibbins (executed for witchcraft in 1656) and Governor John Winthrop, whose death in 1649 coincides with the minister's vigil. Hawthorne wrote two centuries later, in 1849, after losing his post as surveyor of the Salem Custom House when the Whigs won the presidency; he writes of that dismissal in "The Customhouse."

publicationAndReception.publication: Ticknor, Reed and Fields of Boston published The Scarlet Letter in March 1850, with "The Customhouse" as an introductory sketch. A second edition followed within weeks; Hawthorne's "Preface to the Second Edition" (dated 30 March 1850) refuses to change the sketch despite local anger. By Fields's own later account, he persuaded Hawthorne to publish the story as a separate volume rather than in a planned collection of tales.
publicationAndReception.then: The book sold well quickly, and the first printing sold out within days. Reviewers praised its power and artistry; some religious critics, such as Arthur Cleveland Coxe, condemned it as an immoral book about adultery. Salem readers resented the satirical portraits of Custom House officers.
publicationAndReception.now: The Scarlet Letter is among the most taught novels in American high schools and is usually called the first great American novel of psychological and moral analysis. It has been filmed several times (including a 1926 silent film with Lillian Gish and a 1995 film), retold and parodied, and the phrase "scarlet letter" has entered English for any public mark of shame. Modern readers discuss Hester as a feminist figure, the ethics of public shaming, and Hawthorne's own ambivalence toward his Puritan ancestors.

sections.overview: In seventeenth-century Boston, a young woman named Hester Prynne stands on a scaffold holding a baby, with a scarlet "A" embroidered on her dress. She refuses to name the baby's father. The novel follows Hester, her daughter Pearl, the community that judges her, and two men whose connection to her the town does not know.

sections.whyItMatters: The Scarlet Letter asks how a community should treat wrongdoing, what shame does to people, and whether hiding the truth is worse than the original wrong. Students practice tracing a symbol that changes meaning, reading an ironic narrator, and arguing about questions that remain live: public shaming, gender and judgment, guilt and forgiveness.

spoilerOverview.text: The father is the young, revered minister Arthur Dimmesdale. Hester's long-absent husband arrives the day she is shamed, takes the name Roger Chillingworth, and as a physician attaches himself to Dimmesdale, whose guilt is wasting him, and torments him. Seven years later Hester meets Dimmesdale in the forest and they plan to flee to Europe; Chillingworth books passage on the same ship. After his Election Sermon, Dimmesdale mounts the scaffold with Hester and Pearl, confesses, reveals something on his breast, and dies. Chillingworth dies within a year and leaves his fortune to Pearl, who goes abroad and marries. Hester later returns to Boston, wears the letter of her own will, counsels women, and is buried near Dimmesdale under one tombstone with the words "On a field, sable, the letter A, gules."

passage.quote: On a field, sable, the letter A, gules
passage.use: The last line of the novel, the heraldic inscription on the shared tombstone. Read it on day one; ask what a "coat of arms" for a sinner might mean, then revisit it at the end.

flags: First-edition details (2,500 copies sold out in about ten days) are widely reported; check exact numbers before citing them.

Whether Massachusetts Bay actually sentenced adulterers to wear a letter in the 1640s is not certain; a 1694 Massachusetts law and a 1658 Plymouth law prescribed letters. Present the letter as Hawthorne's use of colonial practice, not as a documented 1640s sentence.
The claim that Hawthorne added the "w" to his surname to distance himself from his ancestors is common but not documented in his own words; present it as a widely held view.
Fields's role in persuading Hawthorne to publish the story alone comes from Fields's later memoir (Yesterdays with Authors, 1872); treat it as his account.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “On a field, sable, the letter A, gules” slowly and put it in my own words: The novel's last line describes the gravestone's emblem in the language of coats of arms: on a black field, the letter A in red. Next, craft. I notice Hawthorne uses heraldry, the formal code of noble family shields, for a mark that began as public shame. The strongest word is “sable”: the heraldic word for black turns the darkness of her story into a noble color on a coat of arms. Then, effect. What does the heraldic description on the shared tombstone tell us about how Hester is remembered? My answer: The A has become a kind of family crest: the sign of disgrace now marks a life of endurance and dignity, so the ending leaves us with the letter transformed rather than erased.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Hawthorne wrote the novel in 1849–50, just after losing his job at the Salem Custom House, and he set it in 1640s Puritan Boston, where his own ancestors had been judges. Why might he look back two hundred years to tell this story? Answer: Accept answers such as: to examine the harsh Puritan judgment his family took part in; to question public shaming and hypocrisy; his anger at losing his post shows in "The Custom-House" introduction.

lessonPlan.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
lessonPlan.edition: Standard Ebooks edition (modernized spelling), based on the 1850 Ticknor, Reed and Fields text with the Preface to the Second Edition
lessonPlan.editionNote: The Scarlet Letter was published in Boston in March 1850; the second edition added Hawthorne's preface dated 30 March 1850. The reading text is the Standard Ebooks transcription, which modernizes some spellings (e.g. 'storybooks', 'rosebush'). It has 26 sections: the preface, 'The Customhouse' and Chapters I–XXIV. Cite chapter and paragraph from this edition.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Scarlet Letter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Scarlet Letter: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of The Scarlet Letter has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to sin and guilt.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in The Scarlet Letter. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this chapter, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the chapter on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the chapter to sin and guilt.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the chapter quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in The Scarlet Letter.

objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the novel in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the chapter quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).
Support: one accurate, located quotation that supports the claim, with explanation (1 point).
Complication: one accurate, located quotation that cuts against the claim (ideally the passage named in the key), explained (1 point).
Qualified conclusion: weighs the support against the complication and says how the claim must be limited (1 point).

criteria: Judgment: states how far the claim is persuasive (fully, partly, not), not just agreement (1 point).

The words “scarlet” and “letter” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The narrator calls him evidence of "man's faculty of transforming himself into a devil," and he himself asks "A fiend! Who made me so?" yet says "It is not granted me to pardon.".

Hester casts off the letter. The evidence is “she undid the clasp that fastened the scarlet letter, and, taking it from her bosom, threw it to a distance among the withered leaves” (XVIII: A Flood of Sunshine, paragraph 11). This develops nature and the individual against society: nature responds to their happiness. The words “fastened” and “withered” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Nature shows "sympathy" with "these two spirits," yet Hester has "wandered, without rule or guidance, in a moral wilderness.".

Chillingworth's defeat. The evidence is “Hadst thou sought the whole earth over … there was no one place so secret … where thou couldst have escaped me—save on this very scaffold” (XXIII: The Revelation of the Scarlet Letter, paragraph 18). This develops hypocrisy and truth: the public confession the novel has waited for. The words “scaffold” and “escaped” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Chillingworth admits the scaffold was the one place the minister "couldst have escaped me," and when "Pearl kissed his lips. A spell was broken.".

The novel's moral. The evidence is “Among many morals which press upon us from the poor minister’s miserable experience, we put only this into a sentence:—‘Be true! Be true!…’” (XXIV: Conclusion, paragraph 4). This develops women and independence: Hester counsels women and hopes for a time when relations between men and women will be on "surer ground.". The words “experience” and “miserable” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. She returns because “here was yet to be her penitence,” resuming the letter of her own will, and the narrator’s one moral is “Be true! Be true! Be true!”.

finalPaper.title: The Scarlet Letter: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how Nathaniel Hawthorne develops sin and guilt across The Scarlet Letter. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in The Scarlet Letter and argue how its meaning changes over the novel and why that change matters to public shame and private identity.
Analyze a central character's choices in The Scarlet Letter. Argue whether the novel judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.

Two readers disagree about whether The Scarlet Letter finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of hypocrisy and truth. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the chapter and paragraph (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

Thesis: Specific, arguable and precise; it organizes every section.
Clear and arguable, but broad in places.
States a topic or a summary more than an argument.
Evidence: Accurate, well-chosen quotations from across the work, all cited; meets the requirement.
Accurate and cited, but clustered in one part of the work.
Too few quotations, or some inaccurate or uncited.
Analysis: Explains how specific words, structure and devices create meaning; weighs a competing reading.
Explains the evidence, with some close reading.
Mostly summary; the link to the claim is asserted, not shown.
Organization: Each paragraph advances the argument; transitions show logic.
Order is loose; paragraphs repeat or drift.
Style and conventions: Formal, precise, present tense; MLA format; virtually error-free.
Formal with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.
Informal or error-prone in ways that distract.

finalPaper.exemplar: The preface shows Hawthorne treating his community's judgment with ironic defiance. The text makes this visible when it says “It could hardly have been more violent, indeed, had he burned down the Customhouse” (Preface to the Second Edition, paragraph 1). He says the reaction "could hardly have been more violent" if he had burned down the Customhouse, then announces he will republish "without the change of a word.". A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.

criticalVoices.quote: _The Scarlet Letter_ has the beauty and harmony of all original and complete conceptions, and its weaker spots, whatever they are, are not of its essence; they are mere light flaws and inequalities of surface.
criticalVoices.speaker: Henry James, novelist and critic
criticalVoices.source: Hawthorne (English Men of Letters, 1879), Chapter V, Ch. V
criticalVoices.useNote: Closure: name one "light flaw" you found and argue it is not "of its essence."
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Closing lesson: evaluate the novel's lasting value.
